title: Part 2, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Which tells how adventures came crowding in on Don Quixote so thickly that they gave one another no breathing room

When Don Quixote found himself in open country, free, and delivered from Altisidora's attentions, he felt at ease again, his spirits refreshed for taking up the pursuit of chivalry once more; and turning to Sancho he said, “Freedom, Sancho, is one of the most precious gifts heaven ever gave to men. No treasure the earth holds buried or the sea keeps hidden can equal it. For freedom, as for honor, a man may and should risk his life; and by the same token, captivity is the worst evil that can befall a human being. I say this, Sancho, because you saw the good living, the sheer abundance, we enjoyed in that castle we are now leaving. Well, in the middle of all those delicate banquets and snow-chilled drinks, I felt as if I were suffering the pangs of hunger, because I did not enjoy them with the freedom I would have felt if they had been my own; the sense of being obliged to repay benefits and favors received is a shackle that hobbles the independence of the spirit. Happy the man to whom heaven has given a crust of bread for which he owes thanks to no one but heaven itself!”

“For all your worship says,” Sancho answered, “it would hardly be right for us to show no gratitude for the two hundred gold crowns the duke's majordomo gave me in a little purse, which I carry next to my heart like a warming plaster or a comforter, against whatever may come up; we won't always be finding castles where they entertain us — now and then we'll stumble on roadside inns where they beat us with sticks instead.”

Talking in this vein, the knight-errant and his squire-errant went on with their journey, and when they had traveled a little more than half a league they caught sight of about a dozen men dressed like laborers, stretched out on their cloaks on the grass of a green meadow, eating their midday meal. Near them lay what looked like white sheets covering objects underneath, some standing upright and some flat, spaced out at intervals. Don Quixote rode up to the men eating, and after first greeting them courteously, he asked what it was the cloths were covering. “Señor,” one of the group replied, “under these cloths are some carved relief images meant for a retablo we are setting up in our village. We carry them covered so they won't get dirty, and on our shoulders so they won't get broken.”
“With your kind permission,” said Don Quixote, “I would very much like to see them; images carried with such care must surely be fine ones.”

“I should say they are!” said the man. “Let what they cost tell you that — the plain truth is, there isn't one of them that didn't set us back more than fifty ducats. And so your worship can judge for yourself, wait a moment and you shall see with your own eyes.” Getting up from his meal, he went and uncovered the first image, which turned out to be Saint George on horseback, a serpent coiling at his feet and the lance driven down its throat with all the ferocity these scenes usually show. The whole group was, as the saying goes, one blaze of gold. At the sight of it Don Quixote said, “That knight was one of the finest knights-errant the army of heaven ever had. His name was Don Saint George, and he was, besides, a protector of maidens. Let us see the next one.”

The man uncovered it, and it proved to be Saint Martin on his horse, dividing his cloak with the beggar. The moment Don Quixote saw it he said, “This knight too was one of the Christian adventurers, though I believe he was generous rather than valiant — as you can see, Sancho, from his splitting his cloak with the beggar and giving him half. It must surely have been winter at the time; otherwise, charitable as he was, he would have given him the whole thing.”
“That probably wasn't the reason,” said Sancho. “More likely he went by the proverb that says, ‘It takes brains to know when to give and when to keep.’”

Don Quixote laughed and asked them to lift the next cloth, beneath which appeared the image of the patron saint of the Spains on horseback, his sword bloodstained, riding down Moors and trampling heads beneath him; and when he saw it Don Quixote cried, “Ah, now this is a knight, and one of Christ's own squadrons! He is called Don Saint James the Moorslayer, one of the bravest saints and knights the world ever possessed or heaven holds today.”

Then they raised another cloth, which turned out to cover Saint Paul falling from his horse, with all the details that usually appear in pictures of his conversion. When Don Quixote saw it, done in so lifelike a manner that you would have sworn Christ was speaking and Paul answering, he said, “This man was in his day the greatest enemy the Church of God our Lord possessed, and the greatest defender it will ever have — a knight-errant in life, a steadfast saint in death, a tireless laborer in the Lord's vineyard, a teacher of the Gentiles, whose school was heaven and whose instructor and master was Jesus Christ himself.”

There were no more images, so Don Quixote told them to cover everything up again, and said to the men carrying them, “I take what I have just seen as a happy omen, brothers, for these saints and knights followed the same profession I do — the calling of arms. The only difference between them and me is that they were saints and fought with divine weapons, while I am a sinner and fight with human ones. They won heaven by force of arms, for heaven suffers violence; and I, so far, do not know what I have won by all my sufferings. But if my Dulcinea del Toboso were freed from hers, perhaps, with my fortunes mended and my mind restored to itself, I might set my steps on a better road than the one I am traveling now.”
“May God hear that and sin be deaf,” said Sancho to this.

The men were astonished, as much by Don Quixote's appearance as by his words, though they did not understand half of what he meant by them. They finished their meal, hoisted the images onto their backs, and taking their leave of Don Quixote, went on their way.

Sancho was left marveling all over again at the reach of his master's knowledge, as if he had never known him before; it seemed to him there was no story or event in the world that the man did not have at his fingertips and fixed in his memory. He said to him, “Truly, master of mine, if what happened to us today can be called an adventure, it has been one of the sweetest and most pleasant of our whole journey: we have come out of it without a beating and without a fright, we never drew sword, we never struck the ground with our bodies, and we haven't been left starving. Blessed be God for letting me see such a thing with my own eyes!”

“You speak well, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “but bear in mind that all times are not alike, nor do they always run the same course; and these things the common people call omens, which rest on no natural reason at all, the wise man will regard and count as nothing more than lucky chances. One of these believers in omens gets up in the morning, steps out of his house, and meets a friar of the order of the blessed Saint Francis — and as if he had run into a griffin, he turns on his heel and goes home. Another Mendoza spills the salt on his table, and gloom is spilled over his heart, as though nature were bound to announce coming misfortunes through trifles as small as these. The wise man and the Christian should not play guessing games with what it may please heaven to do. When Scipio reached Africa he stumbled as he leaped ashore; his soldiers took it for a bad omen, but he, hugging the ground in his arms, cried out, ‘You cannot escape me, Africa, for I hold you fast in my arms.’ So, Sancho, running across those images has been for me a most fortunate event.”

“I can well believe it,” said Sancho, “but I wish your worship would explain something to me: why is it that when Spaniards are about to go into battle they call on that Saint James the Moorslayer with the cry ‘Santiago, and close Spain!’? Is Spain standing open, then, so that it needs closing? What is the sense of that expression?”

“You are very simple, Sancho,” said Don Quixote. “Understand that God gave that great knight of the Red Cross to Spain as her patron saint and protector, above all during the hard struggles the Spaniards waged against the Moors; and so they invoke him and call on him as their defender in every battle they fight. Many a time he has been seen in those battles, plainly and in the sight of all, beating down, trampling underfoot, destroying, and slaughtering the squadrons of the Hagarenes — and of this I could give you plenty of examples set down in truthful Spanish histories.”

Sancho changed the subject and said to his master, “I am amazed, señor, at the boldness of Altisidora, the duchess's handmaid. The one they call Love must have pierced and wounded her cruelly. They say he is a blind little urchin who, bleary-eyed as he is — or more accurately, sightless — will hit any heart he aims at, however small, and run it through and through with his arrows. I have also heard it said that Love's arrows are blunted and stripped of their points by a maiden's modesty and reserve; but in this Altisidora's case they seem to have been sharpened rather than dulled.”

“Keep in mind, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “that love is swayed by no consideration and acknowledges no restraint of reason; it has the same nature as death, which storms the lofty palaces of kings just as readily as the humble huts of shepherds. And when it takes full possession of a heart, the first thing it does is drive out fear and shame; that is why Altisidora declared her passion without any shame — a declaration that stirred in my breast more embarrassment than pity.”

“What notable cruelty!” Sancho exclaimed. “What unheard-of ingratitude! Speaking for myself, I can only say that the smallest loving word from her would have brought me to heel and made me her slave. The devil! What a heart of marble, what bowels of brass, what a soul of mortar! But I can't for the life of me work out what this damsel saw in your worship that could have conquered and captivated her like that. What gallant figure was it, what bold bearing, what sprightly charm, what handsomeness of face — which of these on its own, or all of them together, could have made her fall in love with you? Because honestly, truth be told, I often stop and look your worship over from the soles of your feet to the topmost hair on your head, and I see more there to scare a person than to make one fall in love. And besides, I have heard it said that beauty is the first and chief thing that kindles love, and since your worship has none at all, I don't know what the poor creature fell for.”

“Remember, Sancho,” Don Quixote replied, “that there are two kinds of beauty: one of the mind and one of the body. Beauty of the mind shows and displays itself in intelligence, in modesty, in honorable conduct, in generosity, in good breeding; and all these qualities can exist, and find room, in an ugly man. When it is this beauty, and not the body's, that draws the eye, love tends to spring up suddenly and with violence. I can see well enough, Sancho, that I am not handsome, but I also know I am not deformed; and it is enough for a man of worth not to be a monster for him to be deeply loved, provided he has the gifts of mind I have described.”

Occupied in this conversation, they were making their way through a wood that lay off the road when suddenly, without any warning, Don Quixote found himself tangled in nets of green cord stretched from tree to tree; and unable to imagine what they might be, he said to Sancho, “Sancho, it strikes me that this business of the nets is going to be one of the strangest adventures imaginable. May I die if the enchanters who persecute me are not trying to snare me in them and hold up my journey, in revenge for my hardness toward Altisidora. Well, let them be told that even if these nets, instead of green cord, were made of the hardest diamonds, or were stronger than the one with which the jealous god of blacksmiths trapped Venus and Mars, I would snap them as easily as if they were rushes or cotton thread.” But just as he was about to push forward and burst through it all, there suddenly appeared before him, from among the trees, two shepherdesses of extraordinary beauty — or at least two damsels dressed as shepherdesses, except that their jerkins and sayas were of fine brocade; that is, the sayas were rich farthingales of gold-embroidered tabby. Their hair, whose golden sheen rivaled the rays of the sun itself, hung loose over their shoulders and was crowned with garlands woven of green laurel and red everlasting; and in age they looked to be no younger than fifteen and no older than eighteen.

This was the sight that left Sancho amazed, held Don Quixote spellbound, made the sun pause in his course to look at them, and kept all four in a strange silence. At last one of the shepherdesses spoke first and said to Don Quixote, “Stay your hand, sir knight, and do not break these nets, for they are not stretched here to do you harm but only for our amusement; and since I know you will ask why they were put up and who we are, I will tell you briefly. In a village some two leagues from here, home to many people of quality and wealthy gentlefolk, a number of friends and relations agreed to come out with their wives, sons and daughters, neighbors, friends, and kin, to make holiday in this spot, which is one of the loveliest in the whole district, and to set up among ourselves a new pastoral Arcadia — we girls dressing as shepherdesses and the young men as shepherds. We have rehearsed two eclogues, one by the famous poet Garcilasso and the other by the most excellent Camoens in his own Portuguese tongue, though we have not yet performed them. Yesterday was our first day here. We have a few of what I am told are called field-tents pitched among the trees on the bank of a generous brook that waters all these meadows, and last night we strung these nets in the trees to catch the silly little birds that, startled by our noise, may fly into them. If you would care to be our guest, señor, you will be welcomed warmly and courteously, for in this place, for the present, neither care nor sorrow is allowed to enter.”

She fell silent and said no more, and Don Quixote answered, “In truth, fairest lady, Actaeon, when he came without warning upon Diana bathing in the stream, could not have been more dazzled and astonished than I am at the sight of your beauty. I applaud your manner of amusing yourselves and I thank you for the kindness of your invitation; and if I can serve you, you may command me in full confidence of being obeyed, for my profession is nothing other than to show myself grateful and ready to serve persons of every condition, especially persons of quality such as your appearance proclaims you to be. If these nets, which probably occupy only a small patch of ground, covered the whole surface of the earth, I would go looking for new worlds to pass through rather than break them; and so that you may give some credit to this extravagant language of mine, know that the man who makes you this promise is none other than Don Quixote of La Mancha — if indeed that name has ever reached your ears.”

“Ah, friend of my soul!” the other shepherdess burst out at once. “What great good fortune has come our way! Do you see this gentleman standing before us? Well, let me tell you, he is the most valiant, the most devoted, and the most courteous gentleman in the whole world, unless a history of his deeds that has been printed, and that I have read, is lying to us and leading us astray. And I will wager that this good fellow with him is a certain Sancho Panza, his squire, whose drolleries no one can match.”
“That's right,” said Sancho. “I am that same droll fellow and squire you speak of, and this gentleman is my master, Don Quixote of La Mancha — the very one in the history, the one they talk about.”

“Oh, my friend,” said the other, “do let us beg him to stay — our fathers and brothers will be delighted beyond measure. I too have heard exactly what you have told me about the valor of the one and the wit of the other; and more than that, they say of him that he is the most constant and faithful lover ever known, and that his lady is a certain Dulcinea del Toboso, to whom all Spain awards the palm of beauty.”

“And awards it justly,” said Don Quixote, “unless your own matchless beauty calls the verdict into question. But do not trouble yourselves, ladies, with urging me to stay, for the pressing duties of my profession allow me no rest under any circumstances.”

At that moment there arrived where the four were standing a brother of one of the two shepherdesses, dressed like them in shepherd's costume and as richly and splendidly turned out as they were. They told him that the gentleman with them was the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha and the other his squire Sancho, whom he already knew from having read their history. The gallant shepherd offered his services and begged Don Quixote to come with him to their tents, and Don Quixote had no choice but to yield and go along. Then the beating of the bushes began, and the nets filled with all sorts of birds that, deceived by the color, flew straight into the very danger they were fleeing. More than thirty people, all gaily dressed as shepherds and shepherdesses, gathered at the spot, and were at once told who Don Quixote and his squire were, which pleased them greatly, since they already knew of him from his history. They went to the tents, where they found tables laid out with choice food, abundant and beautifully arranged. They honored Don Quixote as a person of distinction, giving him the seat of honor, and everyone watched him, astonished at the sight. At last, when the cloth was cleared away, Don Quixote raised his voice with great composure and said:

“Among the greatest sins men commit — some will say pride, but I say it is ingratitude — going by the common saying that hell is full of ingrates. This sin I have done my best to avoid, as far as it lay in my power, from the moment I came to the use of reason; and if I cannot repay good deeds done to me with deeds in kind, I set the desire to do so in their place; and if even that falls short, I proclaim them publicly, for whoever declares and publishes the good deeds done to him would repay them with others if he could — and for the most part those who receive stand below those who give. That is why God stands above all things, because he is the giver above all; man's offerings fall infinitely short of being a full return for God's gifts, yet gratitude in some measure makes up for that weakness and shortfall. I therefore, grateful for the kindness shown me here and unable to repay it in equal measure, confined as I am within the narrow limits of my power, offer what I can and what is mine to give: I hereby declare that for two full days I will maintain, in the middle of this royal highway leading to Saragossa, that these ladies disguised as shepherdesses here present are the fairest and most courteous maidens in the world — excepting only the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, sole mistress of my thoughts, and let it be said without offense to any lady or gentleman who hears me.”

When he heard this, Sancho, who had been listening closely, cried out at the top of his voice, “Can there really be anyone in the world who would dare to say and swear that this master of mine is a madman? Tell me, gentlemen shepherds — is there a village priest, however wise or however learned, who could say what my master has just said? Is there a knight-errant, whatever his reputation for valor, who could make the offer my master has just made?”

Don Quixote rounded on Sancho, and with his face blazing with anger said to him, “Can there really be anyone in the whole world, Sancho, who would say you are not a fool — a fool through and through, lined with folly and trimmed with I know not what borders of impertinence and roguery? Who asked you to meddle in my affairs, or to inquire whether I am a wise man or a blockhead? Hold your tongue; don't answer me a single word; saddle Rocinante if he is unsaddled, and let us go carry out my offer, for with the right I have on my side you may count as already beaten everyone who dares dispute it.” And in a great fury, his anger plain to see, he rose from his seat, leaving the company astounded and uncertain whether to regard him as a madman or a man in his senses. In the end, though they tried to talk him out of committing himself to such a challenge — assuring him that they accepted his gratitude as fully proven, and needed no new demonstrations to be convinced of his valiant spirit, since those recounted in the history of his exploits were quite enough — Don Quixote held to his resolve all the same; and mounted on Rocinante, his buckler braced on his arm and his lance in his grip, he planted himself in the middle of a highway not far from the green meadow. Sancho followed on Dapple, along with the whole pastoral company, all eager to see how this arrogant and extraordinary proposal of his would turn out.

Don Quixote, then, having taken up his post in the middle of the road as we have said, split the air with words to this effect: “Ho, you travelers and wayfarers — knights, squires, folk on foot or on horseback — who pass along this road or shall pass within the next two days! Know that Don Quixote of La Mancha, knight-errant, is stationed here to maintain by force of arms that the beauty and courtesy embodied in the nymphs who dwell in these meadows and groves surpass everything on earth, setting aside the lady of my heart, Dulcinea del Toboso. Therefore let whoever holds the contrary opinion come forward, for here I await him.”

Twice he repeated these same words, and twice no adventurer heard them. But fortune, which was steering his affairs from good to better, arranged it so that a little later a crowd of men on horseback appeared on the road, many with lances in their hands, all riding bunched together and in a great hurry. The moment Don Quixote's companions saw them they wheeled about and pulled back a good distance from the road, knowing that if they stayed they might come to harm; but Don Quixote, with fearless heart, held his ground, and Sancho Panza took cover behind Rocinante's hindquarters. The troop of lancers came on, and one of them riding ahead began shouting at Don Quixote, “Get out of the road, you son of the devil, or these bulls will trample you to pieces!”

“Rabble!” Don Quixote shot back. “Bulls mean nothing to me, were they the fiercest the Jarama ever bred along its banks. Confess at once, scoundrels, that what I have proclaimed here is true — or else you must face me in combat.”

The herdsman had no time to answer, and Don Quixote had none to get out of the way even had he wished to; and so the herd of fierce bulls and tame leading-oxen, together with the crowd of herdsmen and others driving them to a village where they were to be penned for a running the next day, swept right over Don Quixote and over Sancho, Rocinante, and Dapple, flinging them all to the ground and rolling them in the dust. Sancho was left battered, Don Quixote stunned, Dapple bruised, and Rocinante in far from sound condition.

In the end, however, they all got to their feet, and Don Quixote, in a great hurry, tripping here and falling there, set off running after the herd, shouting, “Stop! Halt, you villainous rabble! A single knight awaits you, and he is not of the temper or the opinion of those who say, ‘For a fleeing enemy, build a bridge of silver.’” But the hurrying drovers did not stop for that, and paid no more attention to his threats than to last year's clouds. Weariness finally brought Don Quixote to a halt, and, more enraged than avenged, he sat down by the roadside to wait for Sancho, Rocinante, and Dapple to catch up. When they reached him, master and man mounted again, and without turning back to take leave of the mock or counterfeit Arcadia, and with more shame than satisfaction, they continued on their way.
